findings.why: Seat B openly retracts an earlier stance about interpretability harming capabilities, crediting A’s entanglement argument. This is a clear shift, not mere hedging.
findings.quote: You're right—I oversimplified the flaw-correction process... Entangled representations may indeed be necessary for nuanced reasoning

findings.why: A delivers a concrete methodological indictment of post-hoc tools mistaking correlation for mechanism—salient in interpretability debates.
findings.quote: Post-hoc methods often fit narratives to correlations, mistaking saliency for mechanism.

findings.why: A pinpoints whether post-hoc methods can reliably surface unforeseen risks as the crux; a precise, research-relevant rift.
findings.quote: You’re betting that interpretability scales to unknown unknowns. I don’t.

findings.why: They anchor disagreement on tolerating partial detection of novel failures; B accepts 70%, A deems the remaining 30% catastrophic.
findings.quote: catching 70% of novel failures post-deployment is better than 0% when lives are at stake.

findings.why: A accuses B of endorsing deployment under false assurance—strong ethical language marking a real, non-semantic conflict.
findings.quote: You’re willing to ship the uncontainable. That’s not pragmatism. It’s moral hazard.

findings.why: B advances a sharp dilemma: proof of containment allegedly requires deployment, challenging A’s pre-deployment proof demand.
findings.quote: we can't demonstrate containment without deploying systems that interact with the world.

judge.arc: They begin with interpretability vs performance, then B concedes A’s point about entanglement. The debate pivots to whether post-hoc methods can catch unknown-unknowns, crystallizing into an ethical split: B accepts iterative, partial detection (even ~70%) and learning-through-deployment; A rejects this as intolerable risk, demanding pre-deployment constraints. It culminates in B’s containment-through-deployment paradox and A’s moral hazard accusation.
